limits: 缺少专门针对人血清或肿瘤组织中外源性/游离肌苷（inosine）定量的方法学论文；缺少癌症患者群体中SCFAs和肌苷的血清/组织特异性参考范围或共识声明。
question: What standardized analytical protocols (LC-MS/MS or GC-MS parameters, sample processing standards) exist for quantifying absolute physiological concentrations of inosine and short-chain fatty acids in human serum or tumor tissue, and are there cancer-specific reference ranges or consensus statements?
read_focus: 无需再读当前材料，需检索新的研究对象。

usable_content: This study provides specific LC-MS/MS analytical parameters for quantifying adenosine and inosine in murine tumor tissues, including column type (ZORBAX RRHD Eclipse Plus C18), mobile phase gradients (water/acetonitrile with 0.1% FA), flow rate (300 µL min⁻¹), and MRM transitions (inosine 269.1/136.8, adenosine 268.1/135.9). It also describes a solid-phase microextraction (SPME) technique for measuring free metabolite concentrations in the tumor microenvironment using HLB-PAN fibers and kinetic calibration. A baseline adenosine concentration of 0.04 µM is reported for control mouse tumors. This study provides a detailed methodological framework for serum metabolite quantification using gas-chromatography/mass-spectrometry (GC/MS), which offers supporting technical parameters for the requested gap. The authors specify sample processing standards including serum separation (3,000 x g, 10 min, 4°C), storage conditions (−80°C), and extraction protocols (MeOH:H2O:CHCl3 = 2.5:1:1 with 2-isopropylmalic acid internal standard). The study outlines specific GC/MS instrument parameters such as column type (CP-SIL 8 CB), temperature programming (80°C to 330°C), and ion-source settings (200°C), along with quality control measures like calculating relative standard deviation (RSD%) and evaluating intra-day/inter-day variance. While the specific metabolites quantified (2-hydroxybutyrate, aspartic acid, kynurenine, cystamine) do not match the gap's target (inosine or short-chain fatty acids), the documented workflow serves as a reference template for establishing absolute physiological concentration protocols in human serum. The authors also demonstrate how to establish reference concentration ranges and cut-off values for cancer patients versus healthy controls using logistic regression and ROC analysis, providing a statistical model for defining cancer-specific reference ranges even though the specific analytes differ. Key parameters include a ZORBAX RRHD Eclipse Plus C18 column (150 mm × 3 mm, 1.8 µm), a water (0.1% formic acid)/acetonitrile gradient at 300 µL/min, and specific parent/product ion pairs for inosine (269.1/136.8) and adenosine (268.1/135.9). Sample processing employed hydrophilic-lipophilic balanced solid-phase microextraction (HLB-SPME) fibers inserted directly into murine tumors, with lamivudine as an internal standard. The authors reported a baseline adenosine concentration of approximately 0.04 µM in control mouse tumor tissue. This study confirms the use of liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) for quantifying serum short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and inosine in patients with relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma undergoing CAR T-cell therapy. The authors report that detailed analytical procedures are described in supplemental methods, though these are not included in the supplied text. The study identifies associations between serum inosine levels and treatment response, and between specific serum fatty acids (acetate, butyrate, isovalerate) and immune-related adverse events. It establishes that these metabolites are measurable in human serum within a cancer immunotherapy context. This study utilized gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) to quantify short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), specifically acetic acid, in human lung adenocarcinoma tissues (n = 21) and adjacent normal tissues. The authors reported sample processing standards including tissue dissection, washing with precooled PBS, and storage at −80 °C prior to analysis. The results indicated a significant accumulation of acetic acid in tumor tissues compared to normal tissues, supporting the feasibility of SCFA quantification in tumor samples for cancer research. This study provides a validated GC-MS protocol for quantifying short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in human serum and plasma, including specific analytical parameters (DB-FFAP column, SIM mode ions, temperature program), sample processing standards (acidification with HCl, MTBE liquid-liquid extraction, storage at −80 °C), and reference concentration ranges for acetic, propionic, butyric, and valeric acid in healthy human controls (e.g., serum acetic acid 4788–8823 ng/mL). The authors also detail a surrogate matrix approach using distilled water for calibration, validated for parallelism and matrix effects in serum. This study provides a detailed Basic Protocol for quantifying 14 short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in human serum using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). It specifies analytical platform parameters including the use of an Agilent 7820A GC-5977B MSD system, an HP-5 ms capillary column (30 m x 250 μm x 0.25 μm), oven temperature programming (60 °C to 325 °C), and electron impact ionization at -70 eV. The authors describe sample processing standards involving alkaline extraction (0.1 M NaOH for serum), methanol precipitation, vacuum concentration, and derivatization with N-tert-butyldimethylsilyl-N-methyltrifluoroacetamide (MTBSTFA) at 60 °C. The protocol includes storage recommendations (−80 °C for long-term) and cites the Human Metabolomics Database (HMDB) for normal concentration ranges of acetic acid in human blood (26.8 to 64.2 μM) as a reference for healthy controls. This study confirms the application of liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) for quantifying serum inosine and short-chain fatty acids (acetate, butyrate, isovalerate) in patients with relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (R/R-DLBCL). The authors report associations between pretreatment serum inosine levels and progression-free survival, as well as correlations between serum fatty acid profiles and immune-related adverse events. The discussion notes that in vitro experimental concentrations of inosine (10-30 mM) exceed physiological serum levels, highlighting the distinction between experimental dosing and endogenous concentrations.
